results.title: Evaluation of an equation at an assignment (Kourovka 14.20)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a group $G$, let $F_n$ be the free group on the unknowns $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$. For an assignment $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in G^n$, evaluation at $x$ is the group homomorphism $G * F_n \to G$ from the free product of $G$ and $F_n$ that is the identity on $G$ and sends $t_i$ to $x_i$ for each $i < n$; it sends an equation $w \in G * F_n$ over $G$ to its value $w(x)$ at $x$.

results.title: Solution set of a system of equations (Kourovka 14.20)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a group $G$, let $F_n$ be the free group on the unknowns $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$. The solution set of a set $S \subseteq G * F_n$ of equations over $G$ is the set of assignments $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in G^n$ such that $w(x) = 1$ for every $w \in S$, where $w(x)$ is the image of $w$ under the homomorphism $G * F_n \to G$ that is the identity on $G$ and sends $t_i$ to $x_i$.

results.title: Evaluating an equation at an assignment
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a group and $n$ a natural number. An equation over $G$ in the unknowns $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ is an element of the free product $G * F(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ of $G$ with the free group on $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$. For an assignment $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}) \in G^n$, evaluation at $a$ is the group homomorphism $G * F(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \to G$ that is the identity on $G$ and sends each unknown $x_i$ to $a_i$.

results.title: Solution set of a system of equations

The solution set of $S$ is the set of assignments $a \in G^n$ at which every $w \in S$ evaluates to $1$.

results.title: Existence of a unit cyclic vector in the GNS space
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a unital C*-algebra with its standard order and let $f$ be a positive linear functional on $A$ with $f(1) = 1$. Let $H_f$ be the GNS Hilbert space of $f$ and $\pi_f : A \to B(H_f)$ its GNS representation. Then there is a vector $\xi \in H_f$ with $\|\xi\| = 1$ such that $f(a) = \langle \xi, \pi_f(a) \xi \rangle$ for every $a \in A$, and the linear span of $\{\pi_f(a) \xi : a \in A\}$ is dense in $H_f$.

results.title: Humps and peaks at a given height in Motzkin paths
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 2$ and $k \ge 1$. A Motzkin path of length $n$ is a sequence of $n$ steps, each up ($+1$), flat ($0$) or down ($-1$), whose partial sums are all nonnegative and whose total is $0$. A hump at height $k$ of such a path is a pair of positions $i < j$ such that step $i$ is up, step $j$ is down, every step strictly between them is flat, and the sum of the steps up to and including step $i$ equals $k$; a peak…

results.title: Height change of a Motzkin step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The three Motzkin steps are encoded as $0 = D$ (down), $1 = F$ (flat) and $2 = U$ (up). The height change of the step encoded by $s \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ is the integer $s - 1$; thus $D$ changes the height by $-1$, $F$ by $0$ and $U$ by $+1$.

results.title: Motzkin prefix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p = p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{n-1}$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$ (encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$), whose vertical displacements are $-1$, $0$ and $+1$, and let $h \in \mathbb{Z}$. The word $p$ is a Motzkin prefix ending at height $h$ when, for every natural number $m \le n$, the sum of the displacements of $p_0, \dots, p_{m-1}$ is nonnegative, and the sum of the displacements of all $n$ steps is $h$.

results.title: Motzkin hump
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p = p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{n-1}$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$ (encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$), whose vertical displacements are $-1$, $0$ and $+1$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and positions $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the pair $(i, j)$ is a hump of height $k$ in $p$ when $i < j$, $p_i = U$, $p_j = D$, every $p_r$ with $i < r < j$ is $F$, and the height after step $i$, that is, the sum of the…

results.title: Unfolding the Motzkin prefix condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p = p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{n-1}$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$, whose vertical displacements are $-1$, $0$ and $+1$, and let $h \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $p$ is a Motzkin prefix ending at height $h$ if and only if, for every natural number $m \le n$, the sum of the displacements of $p_0, \dots, p_{m-1}$ is nonnegative, and the sum of the displacements of all $n$ steps is $h$.

results.title: Bounded Motzkin prefix condition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p = p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{n-1}$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$ (encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$), whose vertical displacements are $-1$, $0$ and $+1$, and let $h \in \mathbb{Z}$. The word $p$ satisfies the bounded Motzkin prefix condition for $h$ when, for every $m \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$, the sum of the displacements of $p_0, \dots, p_{m-1}$ is nonnegative, and the sum of the displacements of all $n$…

results.title: Bounded form of the Motzkin prefix condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$ and let $h \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $p$ satisfies the bounded Motzkin prefix condition for $h$, in which the prefix length $m$ ranges over $\{0, 1, \dots, n\}$, if and only if $p$ is a Motzkin prefix ending at height $h$, in which $m$ ranges over all natural numbers with $m \le n$.

results.title: Characterization of Motzkin humps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, and let $s(p_r) \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ be the vertical displacement of the step $p_r$ (down, flat or up). For a natural number $k$ and positions $i, j < n$, the pair $(i, j)$ is a hump of height $k$ if and only if $i < j$, $s(p_i) = 1$, $s(p_j) = -1$, $s(p_r) = 0$ for every $r$ with $i < r < j$, and $\sum_{r \le i} s(p_r) = k$.

results.title: Motzkin peak
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$, let $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The pair $(i, j)$ is a peak of height $k$ in $p$ when it is a hump of height $k$ in $p$ and $j = i + 1$, that is, when the down step $p_j$ immediately follows the up step $p_i$.

results.title: Peaks are humps with adjacent endpoints
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$, let $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then $(i, j)$ is a peak of height $k$ in $p$ if and only if $(i, j)$ is a hump of height $k$ in $p$ and $j = i + 1$.

results.title: Paths whose last non-flat step is up
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A word $p = p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{n-1}$ of length $n$ in the steps $U$ (up), $F$ (flat) and $D$ (down) has last non-flat step up when some position $i$ has $p_i = U$ and every later step $p_j$ with $j > i$ is $F$. In particular, such a word contains an up step.

results.title: Characterization of words whose last non-flat step is up
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p = p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{n-1}$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$. Then the last non-flat step of $p$ is $U$ if and only if there is a position $i$ with $p_i = U$ such that $p_j = F$ for every position $j > i$.

results.title: Paths whose first non-up step is down
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, each $D$ (down), $F$ (flat) or $U$ (up), encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$. The path has first non-up step down when there is a position $i$ with $p_i = D$ and $p_j = U$ for every $j < i$. In particular, a path all of whose steps are up steps, including the empty path, does not qualify.

results.title: Characterization of paths whose first non-up step is down
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, each $D$ (down), $F$ (flat) or $U$ (up), encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$. The path has first non-up step $D$ if and only if there is a position $i$ with $p_i = D$ and $p_j = U$ for every $j < i$.

results.title: Paths ending with an up step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, each $D$ (down), $F$ (flat) or $U$ (up), encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$. The path ends with an up step when it has a last position, that is, some $i < n$ with $i + 1 = n$, and $p_i = U$.

results.title: Characterization of paths ending with an up step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, each $D$ (down), $F$ (flat) or $U$ (up), encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$. The path ends with an up step if and only if there is a position $i < n$ with $i + 1 = n$ and $p_i = U$.

results.title: Motzkin generating function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Motzkin series is the formal power series $M(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} m_n x^n$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$, where $m_n$ is the $n$-th Motzkin number.

results.title: Standard Young tableau
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A standard Young tableau of order $n$ is encoded by a map $T$ that assigns to each entry $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ a cell $T(i) = (r_i, c_i)$ with row and column indices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The map $T$ is a standard Young tableau when it is injective and, for every entry $i$ and every cell $(r, c)$ with $r \le r_i$ and $c \le c_i$, there is an entry $j \le i$ with $T(j) = (r, c)$.

results.title: Unfolding the standard Young tableau condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ assign to each entry $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ a cell $T(i) = (r_i, c_i)$ with row and column indices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then $T$ is a standard Young tableau of order $n$ if and only if $T$ is injective and, for every entry $i$ and every cell $(r, c)$ with $r \le r_i$ and $c \le c_i$, there is an entry $j \le i$ with $T(j) = (r, c)$.

results.title: Tableaux in the $(2,1)$-hook
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T$ assign to each entry $i < n$ a cell $(r_i, c_i)$ with zero-based row $r_i < n$ and column $c_i < n$. Then $T$ lies in the $(2,1)$-hook when no entry occupies a cell whose row is at least $2$ and whose column is at least $1$, that is, when no $i$ has both $r_i \ge 2$ and $c_i \ge 1$.

results.title: Characterization of tableaux in the $(2,1)$-hook
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ assign to each entry $i < n$ a cell $(r_i, c_i)$ with zero-based row $r_i < n$ and column $c_i < n$. Then $T$ lies in the $(2,1)$-hook if and only if for no entry $i$ do both $r_i \ge 2$ and $c_i \ge 1$ hold.

results.title: Row length of a tableau
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, let $T$ assign to each entry $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ a cell $T(i)$, given by a zero-based row index and a zero-based column index, both in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. For a natural number $r$, the length of row $r$ is the number of entries $i$ whose cell $T(i)$ lies in row $r$.

results.title: First-two-row difference of a tableau
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T$ assign to each entry $i < n$ a cell $(r_i, c_i)$ with zero-based row $r_i < n$ and column $c_i < n$, and let $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ be the numbers of entries $i$ with $r_i = 0$ and with $r_i = 1$ respectively. For a natural number $k$, $T$ has first-two-row difference $k$ when $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 + k$, that is, when $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = k$.

results.title: Characterization of the first-two-row difference
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ assign to each entry $i < n$ a cell $(r_i, c_i)$ with zero-based row $r_i < n$ and column $c_i < n$, and let $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ be the numbers of entries $i$ with $r_i = 0$ and with $r_i = 1$ respectively. For a natural number $k$, $T$ has first-two-row difference $k$ if and only if $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 + k$.

results.title: Standard Young tableaux in the $(2,1)$-hook with given row difference
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, $\mathrm{SYT}_k(2,1;n)$ is the number of standard Young tableaux of order $n$ whose shape $\lambda$ lies in the $(2,1)$-hook, that is $\lambda_3 \le 1$, and whose first two row lengths satisfy $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 + k$ (a missing row has length $0$).

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Use the steps $U = (1,1)$, $F = (1,0)$ and $D = (1,-1)$, and call a word in these steps a Motzkin prefix if none of its initial segments ends below height $0$. For a natural number $n$, this is the set of pairs $(k, p)$ where $k$ is a natural number with $1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and $p$ is a Motzkin prefix of length $n$ ending at height $2k$ that contains a $U$ after which every step is $F$.

results.title: Motzkin prefixes whose first non-up step is down
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Use the steps $U = (1,1)$, $F = (1,0)$ and $D = (1,-1)$, and call a word in these steps a Motzkin prefix if none of its initial segments ends below height $0$. For a natural number $n$, this is the set of pairs $(k, p)$ where $k$ is a natural number with $k \le n - 2$ and $p$ is a Motzkin prefix of length $n$ ending at height $k$ whose first step other than $U$ exists and is $D$.

results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: Where the head sits relative to the tape boundaries: strictly inside the tape, on the first cell, on the last cell, or on the only cell of a one-cell tape. The transition function observes this tag, so the machine can tell the two ends of its tape apart from interior cells.

results.title: Legal head move of a linear bounded automaton
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A move is legal from the head position `h` on a tape of length `n` when the source head is on the tape and the new head position is still on the tape. In particular a left move from an out-of-bounds head is illegal, even though the truncated new head `h - 1` would still be out of bounds: legality requires `h < n` for left moves as well.

results.title: Linear bounded automaton
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A linear bounded automaton: a nondeterministic Turing machine whose tape is the input word. The transition function gives, for a state, the symbol under the head (`none` for a blank cell), and the boundary tag of the head position, the finite set of possible next states, symbols to write (`none` for a blank), and head moves. The boundary tag is what lets the machine detect the ends of its tape: without it the model…

results.title: Initial configuration of a linear bounded automaton

results.title: One step of a linear bounded automaton
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: One step of the machine: choose a transition for the current state, the symbol under the head, and its boundary tag, write the symbol, move the head legally. A step from a configuration whose head is off the tape is impossible: legality requires the source head to be on the tape.

results.title: Nonterminals of the grammar of a linear bounded automaton
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The nonterminals of the grammar of an LBA: a cell, a generator, and the start symbol. A cell records the original input symbol, the current tape symbol, the head state if the head is on the cell, whether the cell is active (simulation acts only on active cells), and the boundary tag of its position (so simulation can apply the boundary-aware transitions).

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The generation rules: the start symbol produces the first cell and the generator (or, for a one-cell word, the first cell alone, tagged `both`); the generator produces a middle non-head cell and itself, or a final right non-head cell. The first cell of a longer word is tagged `left`.

results.title: Activation rules of the LBA grammar
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Simulation rules for a stay move
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Simulation rules for a right move
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The simulation rules for a right move: the head cell rewrites its current symbol and loses the head; the neighbouring cell gains the head. Both cells keep their boundary tags.

results.title: Simulation rules for a left move
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The simulation rules for a left move: the neighbouring cell gains the head; the head cell rewrites its current symbol and loses the head. Both cells keep their boundary tags.

results.title: Conversion rules of the LBA grammar
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The conversion rules: an active cell becomes its original terminal. The head cell converts only in the accepting state, so a terminal word is produced only from an accepting configuration. The boundary tag is discarded on conversion.

results.title: Space-bounded single-tape machines
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. A single-tape Turing machine $M$ runs in space $s$ when, for every input word $l$ of length $|l|$, every configuration reachable from the initial configuration of $M$ on $l$ uses at most $s(|l|)$ cells, whether or not the run halts. The cells used by a configuration are the head cell together with the cells on each side of it up to the outermost non-blank cell.

results.title: Linear bounded automaton
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A single-tape machine is a linear bounded automaton when it runs in space $n + 1$ on inputs of length $n$: every configuration of its run on an input of length $n$ uses at most $n + 1$ cells, whether or not the run halts.

results.title: Space bounds can be weakened
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a single-tape machine runs in space $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $s' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfies $s(n) \le s'(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then it runs in space $s'$.

results.title: A space bound is at least the space of the input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a single-tape machine runs in space $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, then $\max(1, n) \le s(n)$ for the length $n$ of every input word, since the initial configuration on an input of length $n$ uses $\max(1, n)$ cells.

results.title: A machine that, on a blank cell, writes a blank and does not move is a linear bounded automaton
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A machine that, on a blank cell, writes a blank and does not move is a linear bounded automaton. Its head never leaves a blank cell, so it stays on the input or on the two blank cells next to it, and it writes non-blank symbols only on the input. The machine may change state on a blank cell, or halt there.

results.title: Configuration bound
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the configuration bound at $k$ is the number $(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2k}$.

results.title: Configurations of bounded space are finitely many
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, where a configuration uses the cell under the head and the cells on either side of it up to the last non-blank one. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, at most $(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2k}$ configurations of $M$ use at most $k$ cells.

results.title: Space-bounded machines halt within the configuration bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ that runs in space $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. If $M$ halts on an input word $w$ of length $n$, then from the initial configuration on $w$ it reaches a configuration in the halting state in at most $(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2 s(n)}$ steps.

results.title: Halting of a machine running in computable space is computable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, fix any primitive recursive coding of $\Sigma$, and let $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be computable. If $M$ runs in space $s$, then the set of input words over $\Sigma$ on which $M$ halts is computable.

part.title: Conflict serializability
api: A rank increasing along precedence edges gives conflict serializability

results.title: Read or write access
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The kind of access an operation makes to its data item is one of two values: a read or a write.

results.title: Operation of a schedule
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: For $n$ transactions, numbered $0, \dots, n - 1$, and data items of type $X$, an operation consists of a transaction $t \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, an occurrence identifier $k \in \mathbb{N}$, an access, which is a read or a write, and a data item $x \in X$: transaction $t$ reads or writes $x$, and $k$ makes repeated accesses of $t$ to an item distinct operations.

results.title: Conflicting operations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two operations of a schedule conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of the two accesses is a write.

results.title: Operations whose relative order matters
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two operations $a$ and $b$ are order-relevant when they belong to the same transaction or they conflict. These are the pairs whose relative order a conflict-equivalent schedule must keep.

results.title: Conflict equivalence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A schedule $s'$ is conflict-equivalent to a schedule $s$ when $s'$ is a permutation of $s$ and, for any two operations $a$ and $b$ that belong to the same transaction or conflict, an occurrence of $a$ comes before an occurrence of $b$ in $s$ if and only if the same holds in $s'$.

results.title: One transaction before another in a schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a schedule $s$ and transactions $i$ and $j$, transaction $i$ precedes transaction $j$ in $s$ when every operation of $i$ in $s$ occurs in $s$ before every operation of $j$ in $s$.

results.title: Serial schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A schedule $s$ is serial when, for any two distinct transactions $i$ and $j$, either every operation of $i$ in $s$ occurs before every operation of $j$ in $s$, or every operation of $j$ in $s$ occurs before every operation of $i$ in $s$.

results.title: Conflict-serializable schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A schedule $s$ is conflict-serializable when some serial schedule is conflict-equivalent to $s$.

results.title: Edge of the precedence graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a schedule $s$ and transactions $i$ and $j$, there is a precedence edge from $i$ to $j$ in $s$ when some operation of $i$ occurs in $s$ before some operation of $j$ in $s$ that conflicts with it.

results.title: Precedence graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The precedence (serialization) graph of a schedule $s$ of $n$ transactions is the directed adjacency graph whose vertices are the transactions $0, \dots, n - 1$, listed in increasing order, and whose adjacency list at a transaction $i$ lists, in increasing order, the transactions $j$ such that there is a precedence edge from $i$ to $j$ in $s$.

results.title: Serialization of a schedule along a transaction order
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $\sigma$ of transactions and a schedule $s$, the serialization of $s$ along $\sigma$ sorts the operations of $s$ by the position of the first occurrence of their transaction in $\sigma$, where a transaction that does not occur in $\sigma$ gets the length of $\sigma$ as its position. The sort is stable: operations with the same position keep their relative order in $s$.

results.title: A conflict-serializable schedule has an acyclic precedence graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a schedule $s$ in which no operation occurs twice is conflict-serializable, then the precedence graph of $s$ is acyclic.

results.title: Serializing along a complete transaction order gives a serial schedule
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a schedule and $L$ a list in which every transaction occurs. Then the schedule obtained from $s$ by stably sorting its operations by the first position of their transaction in $L$ is serial.

results.title: Serializing along a topological order preserves conflict equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a schedule in which no operation occurs twice, and let $L$ be a topological order of the precedence graph of $s$. Then the schedule obtained from $s$ by stably sorting its operations by the first position of their transaction in $L$ is conflict-equivalent to $s$.

results.title: The serializability theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A schedule without duplicate operations is conflict-serializable exactly when its precedence graph is acyclic.

results.title: A rank increasing along precedence edges gives conflict serializability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a schedule in which no operation occurs twice. If $r$ is a function from the transactions to the natural numbers with $r(i) < r(j)$ whenever the precedence graph of $s$ has an edge from $i$ to $j$, then $s$ is conflict-serializable.
